posts.author: ivory1030
posts.body:
I wanted to experiment with having a far more limited palette in my most recent project, so I made it that each party member just has a single color associated with them that makes up their entire sprite. One of the party members is associated with the color pink, so his sprite looks like this:
This was drawn in Aseprite, and it has a color profile of sRGB. It also shares a sprite sheet with another party member, whose color palette still looks recognizable in the playtest.
Now here's what this sprite looks like in-game:
From what I can see on my primary monitor the colors have all generally been darkened, and the darkest red-pink color has been turned into this muddy orange color. However I have also taken a look at what this sprite looks like on both my secondary monitor as well as my phone, and it's slightly different looking on them too. On my second monitor the red-pink just looks bright red, but on my phone it looks like a slightly less muddied orange. The sprite sheet also looks just fine within the project's files, with it maybe being on the darker end still but at least not orange.
For some additional context, I've actually used this sprite in RPG Maker MV before too. However at the time I was using the Windows 10 OS, and I recently switched to Linux Mint. For whatever reason the color of this sprite looked fine when I was using RPG Maker MV on Windows 10, and I have no idea why switching to Linux would cause that to change. I know it can't
just
be an issue with my monitor because the colors display fine in Aseprite.
I tried fiddling around with the color profile settings in Aseprite but nothing I do seems to change it, so I feel it's specifically a problem with RPG Maker MV. I've also opened up this sprite sheet in a fresh project just to make sure it wasn't a plugin, and it's not. I'd really like a solution to this problem, because it has been driving me up the wall.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
It sounds like a problem with color management or color profiles.
each monitor and each printer has its own way of producing colors, and as a result no two different monitors or printers produce the same base colors.
because this is a problem in professional art and design, all OS have the option of installing color profiles for monitors, picture files and on.
Correctly calibrated they make sure that the colors on monitor and printer are always looking identical no matter on which computer.
Most non-professional people ignore those color profiles as there is no need for them, but it sounds as if your Linux and your Windows are configured using different color profiles (or having never been calibrated at all).
However I can't tell you how the color profiles are implemented under Linux, but that is what you need to look into
